topic: Milestones of Later Modern Indian Sculpture
questionText:
Arrange the sculptural landmarks of post-independence India in chronological sequence:
(A) Amar Nath Sehgal creates the tragic Partition bronze masterpiece 'Cries Un-heard' (1958)
(B) Sehgal completes the monumental bronze mural inside Vigyan Bhavan, New Delhi (1962)
(C) P.V. Jankiram pioneers indigenous sheet-metal sculptures, creating 'Ganesha' (1970)
(D) Aekka Yadagiri Rao carves the four-faced monolithic stone masterpiece 'Chatturmukhi' (1970s)

Choose the correct chronological/logical sequence from the options given below:

options.text: B, A, C, D
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: D, B, C, A
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: A, C, B, D
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

options.text: A, B, C, D
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately identifies the chronological/logical progression.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
The sequence starts with Cries Un-heard (1958), the Vigyan Bhavan mural (1962), Jankiram's Ganesha (1970), and Yadagiri Rao's Chatturmukhi (1970s).
Hence Option C is correct.
Hence, option (D) is correct.

Having witnessed the horrific communal butchery, refugee flight, and butchered trains in Punjab during Partition, Sehgal channeled his anguish into sculpture. In 'Cries Un-heard', three elongated, emaciated bronze figures (a father, mother, and child) throw their heads back and thrust their attenuated arms toward the heavens in an agonizing, silent scream against cruelty. Beyond his art, Sehgal fought an epic 13-year legal battle against the Government of India (Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India, 2005) after his monumental 140-foot bronze mural at Vigyan Bhavan was carelessly dismantled and damaged during renovations. The landmark Delhi High Court judgment upheld Section 57 of the Indian Copyright Act, establishing that an artist possesses inalienable 'Moral Rights' (integrity and paternity) to protect their creation from mutilation, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.
